You have probably noticed that Australian politics keeps producing the same kinds of people. Here is why and what it costs you.

Consider a career trajectory so common in Australian politics it barely registers as remarkable.

A person graduates and goes straight to work in a politician’s office. They learn the rhythms of parliament, build relationships with ministers and journalists, and become fluent in the language of policy without ever working in the field that policy governs. Then they get preselected - often in a safe seat, often with factional support they helped cultivate - and become a politician themselves. After a term or two, they move to a lobbying or consulting firm, selling the access and institutional knowledge they accumulated in the previous two phases.

This is not a scandal in the sense of breaking laws. It is a structural feature of how both major parties recruit political talent. And structural features can be redesigned - if enough people understand what they are looking at.

In the 1960s, the typical Labor MP had worked as a teacher, a union official, or in a trade. The typical Liberal MP had run a business, practised law, or served in the military. They came to parliament having done something outside it.

That has changed. Ministerial offices have become the primary training ground for future MPs on both sides. Staffers attend briefings, develop relationships with departmental secretaries and industry representatives, and build the preselection networks they will later need. Tim Wilson, James Paterson, and John Pesutto all came through the Institute of Public Affairs before entering parliament. On the Labor side, a significant proportion of the current caucus came through ministerial offices or party research roles. Neither party has a monopoly on this. Both benefit from it.

The problem is not that these people lack ability. Some are highly effective. The problem is structural - a system that selects for institutional access and loyalty over direct experience will, over time, produce a parliament that reflects those priorities rather than the communities it represents. A politician who has never managed a ward, run a small business through a downturn, or looked for a rental in a city that has run out of them is systematically less likely to ask certain questions when making decisions about hospitals, small business policy, or housing.

When a former minister joins a firm representing clients in their former portfolio area, they bring relationships and institutional knowledge that took years to build - and that has commercial value. Australia’s rules set a 12-month cooling-off period before a former minister can lobby their former portfolio. For ministerial advisers, the restriction covers only their specific former minister, not the broader government.

These are weak protections. In 2024, former Labor minister Alan Griffin joined a lobbying firm that represents financial services interests within months of leaving parliament. He is not alone. Former Liberal minister Karen Andrews took on advisory roles in the defence sector after her retirement. Both moves were within the existing rules. Both illustrate exactly why those rules need strengthening.

Independent MP Monique Ryan has introduced the Lobbying (Improving Government Honesty and Trust) Bill, proposing a three-year cooling-off period, mandatory ministerial diary publication, and expansion of the lobbyist register to cover in-house industry lobbyists. The Albanese government has not brought it on for debate.

The pipeline runs at state level too, and it matters more than most people realise. State governments control your hospital waiting list, your child’s school, your public transport, and your housing approvals. If state parliaments are insulated from direct experience of those systems by the same professional filtering that shapes federal parliament, the consequences land closer to home. Victoria’s lobbyist register is administered separately from the federal one and has been criticised by integrity advocates as inadequately enforced.

Local government is genuinely different. Councils draw more heavily on people with roots in the community - small business owners, teachers, parents active in local schools, longtime residents. The professional political class is thinner. That diversity is real.

It is also fragile. Developers and industry groups invest heavily in council elections precisely because planning decisions are worth significant money. The pipeline at council level runs not through political staffing but through developer-funded campaigns and industry-aligned candidate networks. The mechanism is different. The result, in contested seats, is often similar.

The question underneath all of this is the obvious one: if the pipeline determines who gets access and who gets ignored, how does everyone else get a seat at the table? The short answer is that access is earned through organisation, not credentials. Parliamentary submissions carry the same formal weight as a corporation’s. Twenty constituents showing up to an electorate office with a specific, evidence-based ask is a meeting a politician cannot ignore. A sharp question at a public event - asked in front of others - is harder to deflect than an email. None of this requires a lobbying firm. It requires showing up in a form that is harder to dismiss than a single voice. Before You Vote has covered the specific mechanics in detail - how to make a submission, how to use the constituent request process, how to organise locally - at beforeyouvote.com.au.

What does this level of government actually control? Ask what they know about their portfolio from direct experience, not just briefings.

What is their actual record? If they came through a ministerial office, the sharper question is: what specifically changed because of your work?

Who is funding them? The pipeline runs on institutional loyalty as much as money. Factional networks and industry-aligned think tanks carry obligations worth understanding.

Who are they accountable to? A politician whose deepest relationships are inside political institutions will return calls accordingly.

What specifically are they promising - and is it costed? Ask the sharper version: when you were a staffer or adviser, who benefited from the advice you gave - and do those same interests benefit from your current position? “I will work collaboratively with stakeholders” is not a policy. It is a description of having meetings.

Three registers. Ten minutes each.

The register of members’ financial interests at aph.gov.au includes your MP’s employment history and directorships. The lobbyist register at lobbyists.ag.gov.au shows which former politicians and staffers are now lobbying in your policy area. They Vote For You at theyvoteforyou.org.au shows the gap between what your representative says about accountability and how they have voted on it.

At the next public event your MP attends, ask: who did you work for before parliament, and where have your former colleagues gone since? It is a reasonable question. Their answer will tell you something.

The pipeline runs because no one asks about it. Pick one register this week. Spend ten minutes. If you find something worth raising, send an email. Then share this with five people who have not seen it.

The class stays small because most people never look. You are looking now.

Your Vote. Your Future.

You know what to do.

Sue Barrett is the founder of Democracy Watch AU and Before You Vote - a free civic education resource for every Australian who wants to cut through the spin. Before You Vote publishes every Tuesday and Friday. If this was useful, share with it to five people.

How can the community independents movement change that dynamic? At Northside Community Voices in the City of Moreton Bay we have begun a process of seeking expressions of interest from people willing to stand in any of the seats in 2028 for Local (12 divisions) State (8 electorates) or Federal (3 divisions). That is a big ask for a fledgling voices group with limited resources. We have set out in our Business Plan a vetting process to ensure we weed out any unsuitable or ineligible candidates but that is only an outline and we would welcome the involvement of someone with you knowledge and experience, Sue, or other voices groups who have a model/template we could borrow and adapt.

Our Business Plan also includes an outline of a Candidate Endorsement Agreement, setting out the expectations and obligations of both parties. Such an agreement needs to cover both the campaign and the period of incumbency, if elected, to ensure the supported representative doesn’t suddenly go rogue, as so many of the One Nation and Clive Palmer people have. Again, we are looking for help in the form of advice and/or a template we can adapt. The community independents can and do sometimes share these resources but we would like to see a more structured approach in place to facilitate sharing and stopping everyone from having to reinvent the wheel. The guidance from your BYV series is really helping, thanks Sue.

Re local government. In Qld. 2026. Three fertile research projects. The Mayoralties of Southern Downs; Ipswich City, and Redland City.
